title: Multi-Agent Failures: Shared Context, Dispatch and Propagation

concepts.heading: Where This Material Comes From
concepts.body: Section 7 is 13 percent of the exam, and it rests on a different kind of source than most of the other sections. The exam guide defines the scenarios, and the Databricks documentation does not define a dispatch protocol, a context propagation mechanism or a schema for sub-agent messages. Treat the terms in this domain as the exam guide's convention and as generally accepted context-engineering practice, never as a Databricks feature you configure. The one documented piece of support is the MLflow Tracing overview: a trace records the inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and cost of every intermediate step, which makes it the evidence you read when you diagnose a multi-agent system. Genie also has a multi-agent page, but it describes a Public Preview capability, so it is never the answer to a question here. The reasoning style is the same as in earlier days: name the symptom, find what information was missing or oversized in some agent's window, and choose the smallest change that fixes it without enlarging any window.

concepts.heading: Insufficient Shared Context and Its Symptoms
concepts.body: A coordinating agent splits a task and sub-agents work on the pieces. Each sub-agent starts with an empty window apart from what it is given, so every fact, constraint and decision it was not given is something it must assume. The exam names three symptoms of that gap. Inconsistent outputs: one writer uses fiscal quarters and another calendar quarters, or two agents use different words for the same entity. Conflicting decisions: a pricing agent accepts a discount that a legal agent, working at the same time, rules out. Degraded reliability: the result changes from run to run because each agent infers what it was never told. The pattern to recognise is agents that each behave sensibly alone and disagree together. Other failures look similar but have other causes: a slow external API, a transient service error and a high token bill do not come from missing shared facts, and passing more context does not fix them. Increasing temperature, swapping models or merging everything into one agent does not supply the missing fact either.

concepts.heading: Dispatch: Task Message Versus Trace
concepts.body: The guide's central diagnosis is a sub-agent that receives an individual task message rather than the full agent trace at dispatch. The task message tells it what to do; the trace tells it what the coordinator already decided, ruled out and learned. Without the trace the sub-agent falls back on defaults, for example quoting a standard refund policy that planning had already rejected. The constraint in the question is usually that the fix must not expand each sub-agent's context window. Pasting a raw, long trace in front of every task breaks that rule, and it also buries the needed facts among exploration steps. The configuration that satisfies both goals is to dispatch a compacted, relevance-filtered version of the trace: the decisions, constraints, definitions and results that apply to this sub-task, in condensed form, with the task message on top. Compaction here is the same technique as in Section 6, applied at the hand-off. To confirm the diagnosis, compare each sub-agent span's recorded input in the MLflow trace with the coordinator's earlier steps and look for what never arrived.

concepts.heading: Context Propagation That Prevents Conflicts
concepts.body: When a multi-agent system produces conflicting outputs, the exam asks which propagation change would most likely prevent the conflict. Two rules cover most items. First, order dependent work. If a staffing plan depends on a demand forecast, do not dispatch both in parallel; run the forecast first and pass its assumptions on, or keep the decision in a shared record every agent reads. Parallel dispatch is correct only for independent tasks. Second, send conclusions together with their basis. A verdict such as margin is acceptable, stripped of the assumption that returns were excluded, can be applied outside the conditions that make it valid; the receiving agent needs the decision, assumptions, constraints and the evidence it rests on, and not the exploration that produced them. This links to context clash, the exam's term for parts of the context that disagree. Prevention beats repair: a later review pass finds the conflict after both agents did the work, while a voting step or a lower temperature only chooses among conflicting inputs and supplies no missing fact.

examPoints: Missing shared context shows as inconsistent outputs, conflicting decisions or run-to-run unreliability; slow APIs, transient errors and cost are different problems.
Sub-agents given only a task message miss earlier decisions; fix it by dispatching a compacted, relevance-filtered trace, not a bigger window or a raw paste.
Order dependent tasks and pass conclusions with their assumptions; these dispatch and propagation rules are the exam's convention, not a documented Databricks feature.

quiz.q: A coordinator dispatches a sub-agent with only the message "Draft the reply for ticket 4411". The coordinator's trace shows the customer's contract was already found to be legacy, so the standard policy was ruled out, yet the draft quotes the standard policy. The sub-agent's window cannot grow. Which change fits?
choices: Switch the sub-agent to a model with a larger window so the full raw trace can be pasted in front of the task
Send the task with a condensed trace slice holding the contract finding and the rejected policy
Add a second instruction sentence so that the sub-agent infers the contract type from the ticket text alone
Let the sub-agent ask the user which policy applies whenever a decision seems to be missing from its message
quiz.explain: The sub-agent lacked decisions the coordinator had already made. A condensed, relevant slice of the trace supplies them within the same window. A larger window with a raw trace is excluded by the constraint and buries the facts, an extra sentence cannot recover what the ticket text never contains, and asking the user repeats work the trace already holds.

quiz.q: A forecasting sub-agent assumes 12 percent demand growth while a staffing sub-agent, dispatched in parallel, plans on flat demand, and the combined plan contradicts itself. Which change most likely prevents the conflict?
choices: Add a review step after both agents finish, so the coordinator reconciles the two plans afterwards
Lower the temperature of both agents so that they pick the same demand assumption on every run
Give the staffing agent more search tools so it can find a demand source on its own
Run the forecast first and hand its growth assumption to the staffing agent before it starts
quiz.explain: The staffing result depends on the forecast, so the decision must reach it before it acts. A later review finds the conflict only after the work is done, lower temperature gives neither agent the other's assumption, and extra tools let each agent choose its own source and may yield a third figure.

recap: Missing shared context makes agents that are sensible alone disagree together. Dispatch a compacted, relevant trace slice instead of a bare task message or a raw paste, order dependent work, and send conclusions with their assumptions. All of this is the exam's convention; MLflow traces are the evidence.

title: Sub-Agent Outputs, Agent Boundaries and Long-Horizon Strategies

concepts.heading: Sub-Agent Output Design
concepts.body: The mirror image of dispatch is what a sub-agent sends back. A sub-agent does its heavy work in its own window, so it should return a distilled result rather than its raw tool output and reasoning. If five research sub-agents each return everything, the orchestrator saturates before it can synthesize, and compressing the text afterwards is too late because the tokens have already entered its window. The exam asks for the output design change that reduces orchestrator load without compromising task coherence, and both halves matter. A one-word verdict cuts load but removes the figures and the contradictions between sources, so coherence suffers. The balanced answer is a fixed output contract: a short, uniform structure with the fields the orchestrator will combine or compare, such as the verdict, key values, references to where the evidence is stored and any unresolved conflicts, with process narrative excluded. Uniform fields also make results easy to merge. The schema idea is the exam's convention and general practice, because the documentation defines no sub-agent output schema. The raw detail stays outside the orchestrator's window, in the sub-agent or in storage.

concepts.heading: Agent Boundary Placement
concepts.body: Every boundary between agents forces a handoff in which the sender compresses what it knows. The exam describes two opposite placement failures. Handoff compression overhead appears when a boundary cuts through tightly coupled work: a writer agent and a validator agent depend on the same reasoning, so every handoff needs a long summary and the receiver still asks for clarification. The signs in a trace are very long handoff messages plus follow-up questions between neighbours. The remedy is to keep the coupled steps in one agent or move the boundary to where dependency is low. Unmanageable context growth appears when a boundary is too wide: one operations agent owns research, report writing, compliance and replies, so unrelated tool results accumulate and accuracy falls over time. The remedy is to split along independent responsibilities so that each agent has a focused window and the coordinator exchanges short results. A larger window or a longer prompt only delays the second problem. Diagnose by reading the trace: long handoffs point to a boundary through coupled work, a swelling window points to a boundary that is too wide. This is the exam's convention.

concepts.heading: Matching the Long-Horizon Strategy
concepts.body: For tasks longer than one context window the exam compares three strategies and ties the choice to the dependency structure of the work. Compaction inside a single agent suits continuous work where each step builds on the running reasoning, since a summary can carry that thread forward. Structured note-taking, an external record of progress and facts that the agent writes and later re-reads, suits work made of discrete milestones where the exact state must survive context resets, for example a progress table of completed tables in a migration. Sub-agents with isolated contexts suit work that splits into independent branches, such as analysing twelve unrelated sources, where each branch is explored separately and reduced to findings. A mismatch produces a recognisable failure: compaction of a milestone list yields a summary like most tables are done, so finished items repeat or are skipped; compaction of independent branches lets every source crowd the others. Trimming oldest messages deletes exactly the early facts, and a bigger window only postpones the problem. These names and the matching rule are generally accepted practice and the exam's convention, not Databricks features.

examPoints: Make sub-agents return a fixed, compact schema (verdict, key values, evidence references, open conflicts); one-word verdicts lose coherence and raw returns saturate the orchestrator.
Long handoffs with follow-up questions mean a boundary through coupled work; a growing window of unrelated results means a boundary that is too wide.
Continuous reasoning fits compaction, discrete milestones fit note-taking, independent branches fit isolated sub-agents; none of this is a documented Databricks feature.

quiz.q: An orchestrator calls six research sub-agents that return their full tool output, and its context saturates before synthesis. A switch to one-word verdicts removed the saturation, but the report lost its supporting figures and cross-source contradictions went unnoticed. Which redesign fits?
choices: Each sub-agent returns a fixed short structure: verdict, key figures, evidence references, conflicts
Each sub-agent returns free-form prose limited to a paragraph, so the orchestrator can read the main points
The orchestrator re-reads all source documents itself after the verdicts arrive, to restore the figures
The team adds more sub-agents so that each one returns an even shorter and simpler verdict
quiz.explain: A fixed contract keeps load low and keeps the fields the report and the contradiction check need. Free prose has no uniform fields and may drop the figures again, re-reading the sources moves the whole load back to the orchestrator, and more sub-agents return still more text to combine.

quiz.q: An agent migrates sixty tables over many hours with compaction. After compactions it sometimes repeats a finished table or skips one, because the summary says most tables are done. Which replacement strategy fits, and why?
choices: Isolated sub-agents per table, because the failure comes from too little parallelism in the migration
Trimming the oldest messages, because the earliest turns hold only setup text that is no longer needed
A progress record read after each reset, since finished tables are discrete milestones
A larger context window, because the summary is only wrong while the window is too small to hold the history
quiz.explain: Compaction yields approximate prose, while a migration of discrete tables needs the exact set of finished ones, which an external structured record keeps across resets. Parallelism is not the problem, the oldest messages contain the completed tables so trimming erases them, and a larger window only delays the loss.

recap: Sub-agents return a compact fixed schema, not raw output and not one word. Long lossy handoffs mean a boundary through coupled work; a swelling window means a boundary that is too wide. Compaction for continuous work, notes for milestones, isolated sub-agents for independent branches.

title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Seven Domains

concepts.heading: Weights and Where to Spend the Last Hours
concepts.body: The exam has 45 scored questions in 90 minutes, and no pass mark is published. The domain weights are D1 Foundations of Context Engineering 16 percent, D2 System Prompt and Instruction Design 9, D3 Knowledge Retrieval and Genie Configuration 20, D4 Memory Architecture with Lakebase and MLflow 18, D5 Tool Design, MCP and Agent Context 13, D6 Context Compression and Compaction 11, and D7 Multi-Agent and Long-Horizon Task Design 13. Together D3 and D4 carry 38 percent, so review them first, then D1, then D5 and D7, and keep D6 and D2 for a last skim. Almost every item is a short scenario with a symptom and a decision; the wrong options are sensible fixes that cost recall, tokens or maintenance. So ask the same questions each time: what is in the window that should not be, what is missing that should be, and what is the smallest change that fixes it. Many terms are the exam guide's own convention, for example poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash, compaction and progressive disclosure, and the docs do not define them; do not look for a product setting behind them.

concepts.heading: D1 to D3: Foundations, Prompts and Retrieval
concepts.body: D1: match the failure to the technique. Poisoning is a wrong fact that persists, distraction is irrelevant material crowding out the task, confusion is too many similar choices, and clash is parts of the context that disagree. Prefer a minimal tool set, just-in-time retrieval and scoped tool results, because attention is a budget and long contexts degrade reasoning. For reasoning modes, weigh the thinking budget against the context it consumes. D2: prefer the targeted prompt revision with the lowest token and maintenance cost, keep few-shot examples only when their marginal contribution justifies the tokens, and judge a larger prompt with tracked experiment results. In Genie, curated example queries and trusted assets, column descriptions and filter expressions beat free text instructions, which are a last resort. D3: fix missing Unity Catalog metadata first, curate the right tables, views and functions into the space, and diagnose AI Search by configuration, chunking and the retrieval failure mode seen in eval logs. Limit retrieval to authoritative, governed sources. Choose pre-inference retrieval when the need is predictable and just-in-time retrieval when the agent must decide what to fetch.

concepts.heading: D4 to D6: Memory, Tools and Compaction
concepts.body: D4: match the memory type to the information need. Durable facts that must survive sessions belong in a Lakebase-backed store, scoped to the subject they describe, while exact task state belongs in a Delta-backed state object and not in an in-context scratchpad. Use structured queries for exact lookups and AI Search for fuzzy recall over text. Compare agent runs in MLflow 3 and pick the configuration that is reliably best, not the single best run. Retrieve dynamically when relevance varies, statically when it does not, and watch for over-retrieval that pollutes the window and under-retrieval that misses facts. Resolve intent before retrieval. D5: disclose tools progressively, write distinct tool descriptions, scope what tool results return, expose logic as Unity Catalog functions, and load Genie Code skills only when relevant. D6: notice the signs that compaction is due, then choose between summarising, clearing old tool results and trimming. Keep decisions, constraints and unresolved items; drop what can be fetched again. Every cut trades fidelity against cost and risk of losing a subtle detail.

concepts.heading: D7 and the Traps to Avoid
concepts.body: D7: diagnose missing shared context from conflicts and inconsistency, dispatch a compacted relevant trace slice rather than a bare task message, order dependent work and send conclusions with assumptions. Have sub-agents return a compact fixed schema, place boundaries where dependency is low, and match the long-horizon strategy to the work: compaction for continuous reasoning, notes for discrete milestones, isolated sub-agents for independent branches. These are the exam's convention and general practice, and MLflow Tracing, which records latency, token usage and cost per step, is the evidence for diagnosis. The traps repeat across domains. A bigger window is almost never the answer, because it delays the problem and keeps the noise. More text in the prompt is rarely right when a targeted change exists. Preview, Beta and Legacy features are not correct answers, and the Genie multi-agent page is Public Preview. Lower temperature, a different model or an added review pass seldom fixes a missing-context cause. Finally, if a question names a constraint such as no larger window or lowest cost, the correct option must honour it.

examPoints: Weights: D1 16, D2 9, D3 20, D4 18, D5 13, D6 11, D7 13; D3 and D4 together are 38 percent, so they get the most review time.
Ask what should leave the window, what is missing, and what is the smallest fix that honours the stated constraint; a bigger window or more prompt text is rarely right.
Most context terms are the exam guide's convention, not Databricks features, and Preview, Beta and Legacy features are never the answer.

quiz.q: An agent trace shows a long window full of old tool results from unrelated tasks, and accuracy falls over time. The team may not use a larger window or a Preview feature. Which first change matches the exam's reasoning?
choices: Raise the temperature so the model explores more of the history before it answers
Add a longer system prompt that tells the agent to ignore the old tool results
Scope tool results, clear stale material, isolate independent work
Switch to a model with a larger context window so the stale results fit comfortably
quiz.explain: The window holds distracting, stale material, so the fix removes or isolates it and honours the constraint. Temperature adds variation without removing anything, a longer prompt adds more tokens to the same window, and a larger window keeps the noise and is excluded by the constraint.

quiz.q: Which statement about the exam domains and sources is correct?
choices: Knowledge Retrieval and Genie Configuration has the highest weight, and several context terms are the exam guide's convention
Memory Architecture has the highest weight, and every context term is a documented Databricks feature that is configured in a workspace
Foundations has the highest weight, and Beta features are acceptable answers when they solve the scenario faster
Multi-Agent Design has the highest weight, because the docs define a dispatch protocol for sub-agents on the platform
quiz.explain: Knowledge Retrieval and Genie Configuration carries 20 percent, the largest share, and terms such as poisoning, compaction and progressive disclosure are the guide's own vocabulary. Memory Architecture is 18, Foundations 16 and Multi-Agent 13, the docs define no dispatch protocol, and Beta features are not keyed as answers.

recap: Spend review time on D3 20 and D4 18, then D1 16, D5 13, D7 13, D6 11, D2 9. In every scenario find what is in the window that should not be, what is missing, and the smallest fix that honours the constraint. Bigger windows and Preview features are not answers.
